title: Ablation of either one or two atria of the heart using dual-energy catheters for patients with longstanding, persistent, atrial fibrillation
official: Pulmonary vein isolation versus bi-atrial linear endocardial dual-energy ablation for longstanding persistent atrial fibrillation: a multicentre randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common heart rhythm disorder and affects around 1 in 200 people. Standard treatment often involves a procedure called catheter ablation, where small areas of heart tissue are treated to prevent abnormal electrical signals that cause an irregular heartbeat.
The standard ablation procedure, known as pulmonary vein isolation (PVI), is effective for many patients. However, it is less successful in people who have had continuous AF for more than a year, known as long-standing persistent AF.
This study aims to compare standard PVI with a more extensive ablation procedure that treats both the left and right upper chambers of the heart. Researchers hope to find out whether this approach reduces the return of abnormal heart rhythms and decreases the need for repeat procedures.

Who can participate?
Adults aged 18 years or over with symptomatic long-standing persistent atrial fibrillation lasting more than 12 months who are suitable for catheter ablation and able to provide informed consent.

What does the study involve?
Participants will be randomly allocated to receive one of two catheter ablation procedures:
1. Standard pulmonary vein isolation (PVI)
2. Bi-atrial linear endocardial dual-energy ablation
Neither participants nor the clinical team assessing outcomes will know which treatment was received.
After the procedure, participants will be monitored to assess whether abnormal heart rhythms return. The main assessment will take place 12 months after the procedure using an implantable loop recorder.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may benefit if the study treatment proves more effective at preventing the return of atrial fibrillation. The information collected may help improve treatment options for patients with long-standing persistent AF in the future.
The study involves catheter ablation procedures, which carry risks associated with heart procedures. Participants will also require follow-up monitoring after treatment.

Where is the study run from?
University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to February 2030

Who is funding the study?
1. Medtronic
2. National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Duncan Fatz, duncan.fatz@nhs.net

interventions.name: The study is a randomised controlled trial, comparing current best practice against the proposed treatment strategy. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Indicated for catheter ablation for documented symptomatic longstanding persistent AF (>12 months duration)
2. Aged >18 years
3. Willing and able to provide informed consent
4. Willing and able to comply with the study requirements
Exclusion criteria:
1. Pregnancy or planning pregnancy
2. Previous AF/AT ablation
3. LA diameter >55 mm in TTE
4. Current involvement in another interventional clinical trial
5. Contraindication to anticoagulation
6. Longstanding persistent AF lasting more than 3 years in duration
7. Cyanotic congenital heart disease
8. Body Mass Index >40 kg/m²
9. No recent cardiac imaging (cardiac MRI or echocardiogram)
10. Severe valvular heart disease

Intra-procedural exclusion criteria:
Re-assessment of PVI after the 20-minute waiting period

Post-procedural exclusion criteria:
Implantable cardiac monitor permanently explanted, during the blanking period
